Two Opus fixtures, 9.35 MB together, reached pushed history this way, and getting them back out took a `filter-repo` rewrite and a force push over a shared branch: `.git` dropped from 12 MB to 672 KB, but the remote still serves each unreachable blob by hash afterwards, because rewriting history does not reach objects already distributed to other clones and caches. ## ⏩ What is not built yet `web/` and `api/` are served from separate hosts today; serving them from one origin once `web/` exists is not built. A Worker deploy that lands while item Workflow instances are running is not handled; a deploy can run a step again, and the item Workflow accepts that for synthesis (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md)). --- Related: [tts-service](tts-service.md) · [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) · [common-package](common-package.md) · [local-development](local-development.md) · [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md) · [authentication](authentication.md) · [invariants](invariants.md) --- title: "TTS service" summary: "Kokoro-82M on Modal, a separate deployable the item Workflow reaches over two web endpoints behind Modal's proxy auth: start a synthesis that uploads its audio to a presigned R2 URL, then poll for its timing." created: "2026-07-29" --- # TTS service ## 🔭 Overview Renders an item's spoken paragraphs to audio on a GPU host, uploads the audio to the R2 bucket and produces their read-along timing. Lives at `tts/app.py`, deployed as its own Modal app (`nagara-tts`), and is invoked by the item Workflow over HTTP rather than imported. Production and local development call the same Modal app. > [!NOTE] The TTS code is an image definition, not a callable library > The synthesis code *is* the specification of the container image that runs on the GPU host: it declares its own base image, system packages, and model bake step, and is uploaded as a unit. It cannot execute inside a Worker; the item Workflow can only invoke it as a separately deployed service. ## ♠️ What it exposes Two web endpoints, both behind Modal's proxy auth, so every request carries the proxy auth headers: | Endpoint | Takes | Answers | |---|---|---| | start synthesis | the spoken forms, one string per read-along unit in unit order; the Kokoro voice, defaulting to `af_heart`; the destination URL, a presigned R2 PUT URL for the item's audio key | Modal's call id for this synthesis, at once | | fetch result | the call id | not ready while the synthesis runs; once it is done, the result below | | Result field | Answers | |---|---| | format | which codec the audio is: `audio/ogg`, or `audio/wav` on the ffmpeg fallback | | duration | the total audio length in seconds, what a progress bar divides by | | timings | one `{start, end}` window per unit, in seconds, the last `end` equal to the duration; see [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md) | The result carries no audio bytes, because the audio is already in the bucket under the item's audio key. The pipeline Worker declares the result's shape as a TypeScript type and trusts Modal's reply to match it; nothing checks it at runtime (see [common-package](common-package.md) for the rule the shared types follow). > [!NOTE] Why Modal uploads the audio instead of returning it > A Workflow step can return about 1 MiB, and a full article's audio is far larger. Handing Modal a presigned PUT URL keeps the audio out of the result, so the result endpoint answers with timing and metadata alone. The pipeline Worker signs the URL with an R2 API token of its own, using common/'s presigning function and its audio key function (see [common-package](common-package.md)). > [!NOTE] Why proxy auth > Modal's proxy auth rejects a request at Modal's edge, before any container starts. A shared key the app checks itself works too, but the web container has to start before it can reject the request. The pipeline Worker holds the proxy auth token as a secret. ## 📩 Flow ```mermaid flowchart LR P["paragraphs[]"] --> S["synthesize each
paragraph with Kokoro"] S --> A["concatenate audio
+ 0.1s gaps"] S --> T["build_timeline:
pause-fold windows"] A --> E["encode: Opus,
WAV fallback"] E --> U["upload to the
destination URL"] U --> R["result: timeline
+ duration + format"] T --> R ``` Each paragraph is synthesized independently through Kokoro-82M and its duration recorded, then the audios are concatenated with a fixed 0.1-second silence gap between them: none after the last paragraph, since there is nothing left to separate it from. [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md)'s `build_timeline` turns those per-paragraph durations into contiguous windows over the same concatenated audio. The encoded audio is uploaded to the destination URL, and the result Modal keeps for the call carries the timeline and the duration; the item Workflow joins the timeline onto the display markdown, described in [article-extraction](article-extraction.md), and never reads text back from the result. > [!NOTE] A newline inside one paragraph string is Kokoro's own split, not this service's > Kokoro splits a paragraph string at each newline before synthesizing it and joins those pieces back with no gap between them; the 0.1-second silence only sits between two separate entries of the `paragraphs` list. So a unit whose spoken form carries several lines, such as a list's items or a table's rows (see [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)), plays as one continuous paragraph audio with no silence added between its lines. The contract does not change. `paragraphs` stays `list[str]`, one string per unit, whether that string carries one line or several. Audio is encoded to Opus through a `soundfile`-then-`ffmpeg` pipeline; if that codec path fails, it falls back to plain WAV. "Playable audio" is the only property either path is judged on, and WAV runs roughly 18 times larger than the equivalent Opus for a full article. GPU and memory snapshotting are both enabled on the deployed class, bringing cold start down from roughly 27 seconds to roughly 6; a container then stays warm for 300 seconds after its last call, to absorb a session's burst of pushes. ## 📡 How the item Workflow invokes it with no broker ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant W as Item Workflow participant M as Modal TTS participant R as R2 bucket W->>M: start synthesis with spoken forms, voice and PUT URL M-->>W: call id M->>R: PUT the encoded audio loop until the result is ready W->>M: fetch result for the call id M-->>W: not ready, or timings, duration and format end ``` The item Workflow's start synthesis step signs the PUT URL and calls the start endpoint, which spawns the synthesis and answers with Modal's call id at once (1, 2). Modal uploads the audio to the bucket when the synthesis finishes (3). The poll step asks the result endpoint for the call id until the result is ready (4, 5), and the store step writes the finished state into the item row together with the tts ledger row, priced by the audio's length (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) and [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md)). The call id and the result pass from step to step as step results; the item row holds neither. Each step gets 3 attempts: start synthesis has 2 minutes per attempt and each poll 1 minute. A synthesis that fails every time fails the item once the poll step has used its attempts, and so does a result Modal has discarded, which happens 7 days after the call. > [!WARNING] A start repeated after a deploy synthesizes twice > Modal accepts no idempotency key and no caller-chosen call id, so a start synthesis step that runs again after a deploy spawns a second synthesis. The cost is one extra synthesis, which is accepted. > [!NOTE] Why the compute platform is the async layer, and there is no broker > The platform's own invocation primitives (spawn plus a non-blocking result read, exposed as the two endpoints) are sufficient async infrastructure at this scale: the running-versus-crashed distinction comes for free from the result read, not from anything the item Workflow tracks separately. The execution layer is coupled to Modal as a result: moving off it means replacing both the compute host and the async layer, and the GPU with them. A single API key is the user's identity, and it guards every route that touches an item. ## ⚙️ Implementation details The API Worker checks the key once, in front of every route under `/items`, so no handler checks it individually; a missing or wrong key answers `401`. The bucket stays private: every way to read it is a link minted to an authenticated caller, and those links expire. Only a backend holds the API key. API->>API: sign a GET URL for one hour API-->>Backend: 307 to the presigned URL Backend-->>Browser: the presigned URL Browser->>R2: GET the presigned URL, no header R2-->>Browser: audio bytes ``` > [!NOTE] Why the route mints a link instead of gating the bytes > A browser `

# Article extraction ## 🔭 Overview The item Workflow fetches an article's HTML, runs the domain's [recipe](recipes.md) on it, and turns what comes back into the list of typed units that every later step reads. The recipe returns a title and markdown units: paragraphs, code blocks and declared images. The item Workflow derives each text unit's spoken form from its display markdown, drops a unit whose spoken form has nothing to say, and acquires each declared image. The result is one list in which every unit carries its `display`, its `type` and its `spoken` form (see [item-contract](item-contract.md)); what a described unit says comes from [image-and-code-describer](image-and-code-describer.md). ## 🌐 Fetching the page The item Workflow's fetch step scrapes the page through Firecrawl with its own fetch-based client. Its raw HTML goes to the recipe step unsegmented. The domain of the final URL, after redirects, picks the recipe. A scrape that cannot reach Firecrawl, or returns no HTML, fails the step; once the step has used its 3 attempts the item fails, with `current_step` naming fetch (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md)). The fetch step writes what each scrape bills, from Firecrawl's `creditsUsed`, as a ledger row (see [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md)), so a failed item still records the credit it spent. > [!NOTE] What firecrawl is called with, and why rawHtml > The scrape asks for `rawHtml` and `markdown` at `proxy: "auto"`. The fetch step asks for `rawHtml` rather than firecrawl's cleaned HTML because the cleaning throws away images (9 against 5 on one corpus article), and the recipe declares the article's images from the page's own markup. `markdown` costs no extra credit, so the fetch step requests it as evidence; nothing reads it. `proxy: "auto"` bills 1 credit when a basic proxy suffices and 5 on a stealth escalation. > [!WARNING] firecrawl's output is non-deterministic > The same URL scraped minutes apart returned a 5x spread in size, and `rawHtml` is post-JavaScript, so it can carry hydrated page chrome a plain fetch never had. The recipe's container and ignores are what keep that chrome out of the units. The spread affects re-recording a test cassette, never a replay, which returns recorded bytes verbatim. ## 📩 How the recipe's units become typed units ```mermaid flowchart TD start(["The recipe returns
a title and
display units"]) --> loop subgraph loop ["For each recipe unit,
in document order"] direction TB kind{"Image unit?"} kind -->|No| spoken["1 Derive the spoken
form from the display"] spoken --> test{"2 Drop rule
matches?"} test -->|Yes| drop["3 Drop: no typed unit"] test -->|No| keep["4 Keep as a typed
paragraph or code unit"] kind -->|Yes| stash["5 Hold it after the
last kept text unit"] end loop --> acquire["6 Acquire held images,
interleave with kept units"] acquire --> any{"7 Any unit survives?"} any -. no .-> fail(["Fail the item:
no surviving units"]) any -->|Yes| write["8 Write the units
into the item row"] write --> next(["Describe, synthesis,
store: survivors only"]) ``` Steps 1 to 5 run at the end of the item Workflow's recipe step, on the units the recipe returns. Steps 1 and 2 are in a required order, because the drop rule reads the spoken form. The loop must also run in document order, because step 5 anchors an image to the last text unit kept so far. When that unit is dropped, the image anchors to the kept unit before it. An image that comes before every text unit goes first in the list. Step 6, the images step, acquires the held images and drops any that will not acquire (see below). Step 7 fails the item when nothing survives, before the list is written. Step 8 writes the survivors and the degradations into the item row as soon as the step has them, and the later steps read them from there. The recipe step writes the title into the row together with its units. A recipe the agents authored or revised is written as its next version by the item Workflow itself (see [recipes](recipes.md)). From step 8 on, describe, synthesis and store work on the survivors only and never drop a unit, so the length guard at store compares one list against its own timeline (invariant 2). > [!NOTE] Why the display list is persisted rather than re-extracted > The display list is written onto the item row as the steps produce it and joined onto the timing at store (see [item-contract](item-contract.md)) rather than re-fetched and re-extracted when synthesis completes. Re-extracting risks a different result across the async gap: the same URL a minute later is not guaranteed to produce the same page. The API shows the units only once the item is `ready`. The unit list's shape, including `ImageUnit`, is a type in common/ that both Workers build against (see [common-package](common-package.md)). ## 🗣️ Deriving the spoken form The spoken form is derived from the unit's display markdown by walking its CommonMark token tree, so the display and spoken forms come from one extraction (invariant 1). A fenced code block becomes the fixed placeholder `"Code sample."`. A table is spoken as its body rows only, each row as its own line of header-aware prose (`"Feature: Extraction, Status: done."`) and never as pipe characters. The header row gets no line of its own. A row gets a full stop only when it does not already end in `.`, `!` or `?`. A cell goes through the same inline walk as a paragraph, so a code span keeps its text, and then through the sanitize tail, described below. A heading and a quote are read as their words, without their markers. Every block inside a unit becomes its own line, so a unit carrying several paragraphs or list items never runs the last word of one into the first word of the next. A list item gets no full stop. An ordered item keeps its `1.` at the start of its line, and the spoken form does not announce nesting depth. A code block or an image nested inside a list unit is silent in the spoken form. It stays inside the list's own display and is never described or acquired on its own (see [markdown-units](markdown-units.md)). A list item that holds only a code block, an image or a nested list gets no line. The derivation strips a task-list checkbox and reads struck-through text as its words, with no sign of the strike. Emphasis markers and link destinations are dropped throughout. A shared sanitize tail then turns any leftover emphasis or code marker that touches text into a space, so the newlines between a unit's lines survive the pass. It drops the space a marker left before punctuation and collapses whitespace. It reduces an opening or closing tag around a word to the word inside (`` to "software", `` to "div"). A lone `<` or `>` is not a tag, so this step leaves it for the operator rule that follows. A last pass turns a comparison-operator sequence into the word it stands for, longest match first: `<=` "less than or equal to", `>=` "greater than or equal to", `->` "to", `=>` "to", `<-` "from", `<<` "much less than", `>>` "much greater than", `<3` "heart", then the bare `<` "less than" and `>` "greater than". `<3` becomes "heart" only when no digit follows, so `<30` reads "less than 30". The pass puts a space on each side of every word it inserts, so `a` and a describable image's with `Image: `; a code block keeps the floor `"Code with no description."` only when the describer fails or the per-item budget is spent. > [!NOTE] The words inside a surviving tag are the article's own > An author writing about software writes ``, `` or `` as text, and a tag still present in a unit's markdown is prose the author escaped. Dropping it silently loses a word the article meant to say, and a whitelist of real HTML element names would be actively wrong here, since an author writing about `
` intends the listener to hear "div". ## 🗑️ Dropping a unit with nothing to say ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Text unit from the recipe,
with its spoken form"] --> C{"Spoken form has a
letter or digit?"} C -->|No| D((Drop)) C -->|Yes| K((Keep)) ``` The rule runs on every paragraph and code unit the recipe returns and reads only the spoken form: a letter inside a link URL or a code block's language tag never keeps a unit. "Letter or digit" follows Unicode, so non-Latin text is kept. An empty spoken form fails the same test. A dropped unit never becomes a typed unit, so its display, its spoken form and its timing window leave together (invariant 2), and it leaves no trace: no degradation, no log. What the rule catches is a section-break ornament (`❦`, `* * *`, `§`) or bare punctuation that a recipe emitted as its own paragraph. A code unit always passes, because its spoken form is the `"Code sample."` placeholder. > [!NOTE] Why a drop leaves no trace > The rule drops only units whose spoken form carries no letter or digit, so what disappears is never a word the author wrote. A degradation records content the item lost, and an ornament carries no content. > [!WARNING] A unit with nothing to pronounce crashes synthesis > The synthesizer produces no audio for a paragraph made only of a symbol, and the TTS service fails the whole call on it. A sockpuppet.org recipe that kept its `❦` section breaks as paragraphs failed its items at synthesis while every extraction step reported success. The drop is what keeps such a unit from reaching synthesis. > [!TIP] Rejected: echoed-title and navigation-label matching on recipe units > The recipe already names the title element and carries the ignore list the author agent wrote, so an echoed title or a "Contents" label is the recipe's to exclude. Matching them again after the recipe step would add a heuristic that repeats a decision the recipe already makes. ## 🖼️ Article images: acquisition and spoken form The recipe declares which images belong to the article: each image unit carries its `src` and `alt`, and the images step acquires exactly the images the recipe declares, with no selection of its own. Each acquired image gets a spoken form and goes after the text unit it followed in the page. Each image is an `ImageUnit` with its own spoken form and therefore its own timing window. ### ⬇️ Acquisition: download, validate, re-encode, store A declared image is downloaded under a per-host semaphore (default 2) beneath a global one (default 10), with a 10-second timeout and a 10 MB streamed size cap. The per-host bound is the one that matters: one article's many same-host images must never open that many connections to a server nagara has no relationship with. A Workers instance holds 6 outbound connections at a time, so at most 6 downloads run at once whatever the global bound. Validation runs on the **decoded bytes**, never on HTTP or HTML metadata. The bytes are sniffed for an `= 200`**, measured on the decoded file. What survives is re-encoded to WebP through the same binding. Each kept image is stored once per content hash, taken over the stored bytes, under the images prefix of the R2 bucket, with its content type on the object, and the hash becomes the unit's image reference, so no origin URL leaks into persisted markdown. common/'s image key function builds the object's key from the hash (see [common-package](common-package.md), and [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md) for the bucket layout). > [!NOTE] Why validate by decoding, not by trusting the attributes or the Content-Type > Most of the corpus omits `width`/`height` entirely (all four New Yorker contact sheets carry neither), and a Content-Type header can lie, so the only trustworthy size and format come from decoding the file itself. The 200 px floor sits in a gap in the corpus: avatars and tracking pixels cluster around 40 px and every legitimate figure is 305 px or larger. Two square brand logos survive it, accepted rather than chased, because a square-ratio rule has no legitimate square image in the corpus to test against and a false positive costs only one cheap describe call. An SVG stays an SVG. Its scripts are stripped before it is stored, and it is stored under the content hash of the stripped markup, with the SVG content type on the object. It has no pixel size to measure, so the 200 px floor does not apply to it. It is describable from its markup (see [image-and-code-describer](image-and-code-describer.md)) and is served like any other image; a client shows it only through an `` element, where its scripts would not run (see [item-contract](item-contract.md)). > [!TIP] Rejected: an image library inside the Worker > The Images binding rejects every SVG, so rasterising one would take a WebAssembly rasteriser in the Worker: about 1.5 MiB gzipped added to the bundle, and every text element in the SVG disappears unless a font is bundled with it. Decoding a raster above about 10 MP inside the Worker exceeds its 128 MB of memory and ends the invocation where no code can catch it. The binding decodes rasters outside the Worker's memory, and a browser renders an SVG natively, so keeping the SVG needs no rasteriser at all. ### 💬 An image's spoken form An acquired image speaks its alt verbatim as `Image: `, or the floor `"Image with no description."` when the alt is empty. The good-alt filter decides whether the describer replaces that form with a generated sentence (see the precedence in [image-and-code-describer](image-and-code-describer.md)). One of its checks is the cruft test: an alt that repeats the article title, or carries no letter or digit, is not a good alt. ### ❌ An image that will not acquire is dropped from both lists An image that 404s, times out, exceeds the size cap, will not decode, or fails to process through the Images binding is dropped from `display` and `spoken` alike (invariant 2), and the drop is recorded as a `degradation`: a typed object `{"type": "image", "url": , "reason": }` that never rides on the wire. This is acquisition failure only, kept distinct from a **describe** failure, which never goes silent (see [image-and-code-describer](image-and-code-describer.md)). The two divide by layer: an image that never arrived has no unit to speak for, so it drops; an image that arrived but could not be described keeps a spoken fallback. > [!NOTE] Why a degradation column, when the item is still `ready` > `error` stays failed-only, and that rule is worth keeping. A `ready` item that silently dropped six of twelve images exposes nothing to the client and a full record to the operator: technically `ready` and quietly worse. The degradation list is what makes that visible without failing the item. Its scope is runtime degradations only. ## ⏩ What is not built yet - **Prose-boilerplate stripping.** Footer donation asides and sponsor mentions arrive as full sentences and reach the audio unless the recipe ignores them. The item Workflow does not filter them, because a generic filter risks trimming real content. - **Quote voice switching.** A listener hears a quote in the one narrator voice, and nobody has yet validated the blockquote audio round-trip end to end. --- Related: [recipes](recipes.md) · [markdown-units](markdown-units.md) · [image-and-code-describer](image-and-code-describer.md) · [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) · [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md) · [item-contract](item-contract.md) · [tts-service](tts-service.md) · [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md) · [common-package](common-package.md) · [invariants](invariants.md) · [what-gets-read-aloud](../product-design/what-gets-read-aloud.md) --- title: "Recipes" summary: "How one agent-authored script per domain extracts the domain's articles into markdown units, its versioned record, how a URL matches to it, and how agents author and revise it." created: "2026-09-13" --- # Recipes ## 🔭 Overview A recipe is one domain's extraction knowledge: a script that receives an article's HTML as a Cheerio document and returns the article as a title and a list of markdown units, deterministically, so the same page always yields the same units. Agents write recipes. The first article from a domain authors the domain's recipe, and every later article extracts with it. When a recipe fails an article, that article triggers a revision. The model runs at authoring time only. ## 🧾 The script and its declarations A recipe is a script plus the declarations around it. The container selector names the element that contains the article, and everything outside the container is site chrome. The inventory names every element kind the domain's pages carry inside the container and the role each plays: a unit, inline content, a wrapper, or the title. The ignores are the selectors deliberately excluded, each with the judgement that justified it; typical ignores are ads, date stamps and share rows. Every recipe excludes footnote markers and footnote bodies, because the authoring prompts instruct it to. The author prompt and the revision prompt embed one shared contract of plain instructions. The prompts also require GFM markdown. They have the recipe replace every `` element with its alttext as plain text, with no delimiter, before calling `toMarkdown`. The rule covers a block formula and an inline one in a paragraph, list item, table cell or quote alike. The recipe passes the whole element to `toMarkdown`, never a piece of it, and declares a whole list as one unit even when the list holds a code block or an image. They exclude a blockquote's attribution, a `
`, a heading self-link and a heading that repeats the title, and they keep a task list's checkboxes. See [markdown-units](markdown-units.md) for what each of those becomes in a unit's display. The inventory is the union across the domain's pages, and an element kind absent from one page is normal variation across a domain's posts. The script receives the Cheerio document and `toMarkdown`, the fixed HTML-to-markdown converter, from the runtime, and imports nothing. The script reads the document without changing it. Domain knowledge enters as structural preparation of a cloned element. The script builds a `` for a table that lacks one, swaps MathML for the LaTeX in its `alttext`, removes footnote subtrees, and wraps a span-built listing in a `
`. The fixed pass converts the prepared clone.

> [!TIP] Rejected: the agent writes its own conversion
> A trial where the agent hand-converted html to markdown matched the fixed pass on quality and gained nothing by it: conversion stopped being identical across domains, and a recipe could get conversion wrong. The per-domain tricks survived as clone preparation, which is reviewable DOM structure, never a rewritten converter.

## 📦 Units and the fixed pass

Units come back in document order, one element per unit as the recipe declares them, never overlapping: once an element is a unit, everything inside it is that unit's content. The kinds are `paragraph`, `code` and `image`. A paragraph is any flow that renders as markdown: prose, headings, quotes, lists, tables; a list is a single declared unit, even one holding a code block or an image; the nested code block or image stays inside the list's own markdown and never becomes a unit of its own (see [markdown-units](markdown-units.md)). The fixed conversion pass produces a paragraph or code unit's display markdown. An image unit carries `src` and `alt` exactly as the page presents them: the recipe never invents `alt`, and the src is how the recipe resolves the domain's lazy-load conventions. An image the article carries is always emitted, even when its src cannot be resolved. Acquiring, validating, describing or dropping images is downstream's business.

> [!NOTE] Why three kinds and not one per markdown shape
> Downstream distinguishes exactly three things: text rendered as markdown and read as prose, code that gets described instead of read, and images that get acquired and follow the alt precedence. Headings, quotes, lists and tables all derive their display from their markdown, so one paragraph kind covers them; even the read-along table of contents derives from a `#`-prefixed unit's display text, not from a kind.

The same validator runs at authoring, revision and extraction. It checks that every unit's element is inside the container, in document order, none nested inside another; that every element kind in the container is declared or reported as unexpected; that no readable text is left after the units and ignores are removed, with the leftover report naming the element kinds that carry it; and that no declared unit is an `
  • ` on its own. The report line for an orphaned `
  • ` names the unit, the list it belongs to and the rule that a recipe hands a list over whole. It also checks that every unit's markdown is valid: non-empty, no residual HTML outside code, balanced fences. The fence check accepts an opening fence right after a list, quote or task marker, because a list item holding only a code block puts the fence on the marker's own line. Invalid markdown fails a recipe like any other problem.

## 💽 The recipe record

```mermaid
erDiagram
    RECIPE_VERSION ||--o{ ITEM : extracts
    RECIPE_VERSION {
        string id PK
        string domain
        int version
        text script
        datetime created_at
    }
    ITEM {
        string recipe_version_id FK "nullable"
        string extraction_domain
    }
```

Each version of a domain's recipe is one row in the `recipe_versions` table of the D1 database the items share, and the item Workflow writes it. Its shape is a type in common/, and common/'s SQL migrations create the table (see [common-package](common-package.md)). A revision is a pure insert that updates no row, and the current recipe for a domain is the highest version, so the per-article read is one indexed descent. The `script` column carries the entire recipe with its declarations embedded, stored exactly as the authoring loop validated it and kept whole so a failing recipe reaches a prompt as one piece. `id` is a generated string following the house pattern. Extraction sets `recipe_version_id` on the item to the version whose script extracted it. That link traces a revision that made things worse to the items it touched. The column is null for items that never reached extraction. Recipes are global: one recipe per domain, shared by every listener.

> [!TIP] Rejected: a current flag or a separate history table
> A flag mutates the previous row and is denormalized state that can disagree with the version number; a current-plus-history pair overwrites the payload in place and duplicates the schema.

## ⚖️ Matching a URL to a recipe

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Article URL arrives"] --> B["Fetch it, redirects
    resolve"]
    B --> C["Host of the final URL,
    leading www dropped"]
    C --> D{"Any recipe version
    for that domain?"}
    D -->|"No"| E["Author one: the base prompt
    against this article"]
    E --> F{"Authoring succeeded?"}
    F -->|"No, after its one retry"| N(("Nothing: the
    item fails"))
    F -->|"Yes"| G["Save it as the domain's
    version 1"]
    D -->|"Yes"| H["Current version:
    the highest"]
    G --> R(("The recipe to
    extract with"))
    H --> R
```

The key is the host of the fetch's final URL with only a leading `www` dropped: subdomains are distinct domains, so `blog.exe.dev` and `exe.dev` hold separate recipes, and a canonical link declared inside the page does not change it. Consolidation comes from redirects: a hundred domains redirecting to one place all land on that domain's recipe. No recipe serves a set of domains, and platform-hosted hostnames with identical markup each author their own.

> [!NOTE] Why no recipe serves several domains
> Platform-hosted blogs put many hostnames on identical markup, and one recipe describing that markup would save every later hostname its authoring run. Sharing was rejected to keep one recipe per domain strict: a recipe's identity is its domain's key, and a set-valued key complicates matching, storage and revision for a cost, repeated authoring, that only platforms pay.

## 📩 The lifecycle: authoring and revision

First authoring happens when a domain's first article arrives: the base prompt runs against that article's HTML, best-effort within one hundred turns, with one retry of the whole run, and if that fails the item fails with nothing saved for the domain. A domain's homepage enqueued by mistake fails and saves nothing, and the next real article authors fresh.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor L as Listener
    participant P as Item Workflow
    participant A as Agent
    participant V as Recipe runtime
    participant S as D1

    L->>P: Enqueues the article URL
    P->>P: Extract with the current version
    P->>P: Validation fails
    P->>A: Iteration prompt, current script and report
    Note over P,A: The domain is locked, its other articles hold
    alt the page is not an article
        A-->>P: The verdict
        P-->>L: Item fails, the recipe stands
    else a fix
        A->>V: Run the fix against this article
        loop within 100 turns, then two retries of the run
            V-->>A: Report
            A->>A: Fix additively, re-validate
        end
        V-->>A: Problems none
        A-->>P: The passing script
        P->>S: Insert as the new highest version
        P->>P: The held item re-extracts with the new version
        P-->>L: Item proceeds
    else the fix gives up
        A-->>P: No passing version
        P-->>L: Item fails, the old version stays current
    end
```

Revision triggers when an article fails validation under the current version. The iteration prompt receives the current script, stored whole, and the validator's report. The standing instruction is additive: keep the recipe's previous assumptions and add what this article needs. The exception is a wholesale markup change, where the agent judges the domain was redesigned and may rewrite the recipe outright. Validation is against the triggering article only. The item that triggered the revision holds while the revision runs, then retries with the new version; the listener sees a slow item and nothing else. Authoring and revision both run inside the item Workflow's recipe step, while the item holds its domain's lease (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md)). Each attempt of the recipe step has 15 minutes; one measured authoring run took 97 s, and the hundred-turn bound is stated in the prompt alone. A revision that gives up writes no version, so the older one stays current and the next article from the domain triggers revision again. Each attempt is independently bounded.

> [!WARNING] A failed revision leaves the domain exposed
> Every new article from a permanently broken domain triggers one bounded revision attempt before failing, and nothing counts these consecutive attempts: the failures are visible, but the agent spend is unbounded.

> [!NOTE] The not-an-article verdict is what catches the 200-status error page
> A URL serving an HTTP 200 error page extracts cleanly under a generic extractor and reaches `ready` as audio of the error page. An agent looking at the page to author or revise reports the page for what it is. The verdict fails the item, from either prompt, without retrying the recipe step. From revision, the verdict also means no version is written and the recipe stands.

## ♠️ What extraction hands the pipeline

| Input | What it is | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| The article's HTML | Firecrawl's rawHtml for the URL | The item Workflow's fetch step, which resolves redirects and so decides the domain |
| The recipe | The domain's current version, the script stored whole | The `recipe_versions` table in D1, by the matched domain |

| Output | What it carries |
|---|---|
| The title | The article's own title; the agent prefers the element that contains it, its judgement when there is none |
| The units | `{ kind, markdown or src+alt }`, document order |
| The verdict | Empty when extraction succeeded; not-an-article or not-accessible fails the item |

The recipe's markdown is the single source of truth: display shows it as-is; the spoken form derives from it generically and never reaches a client, and the item Workflow drops a unit whose spoken form has no letter or digit (see [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)). The image handler receives the recipe-declared images, acquires and validates them, and prefers a good alt, then a generated description. When acquisition fails, it drops the image with a degradation. The `og:image` lede has no generic rule; when a page's `og:image` belongs in the article, declaring it is the recipe's judgement.

Production and local development call the same Modal app. 129 130 > [!NOTE] The TTS code is an image definition, not a callable library 131 > The synthesis code *is* the specification of the container image that runs on the GPU host: it declares its own base image, system packages, and model bake step, and is uploaded as a unit. It cannot execute inside a Worker; the item Workflow can only invoke it as a separately deployed service. 132 133 ## ♠️ What it exposes 134 135 Two web endpoints, both behind Modal's proxy auth, so every request carries the proxy auth headers: 136 137 | Endpoint | Takes | Answers | 138 |---|---|---| 139 | start synthesis | the spoken forms, one string per read-along unit in unit order; the Kokoro voice, defaulting to `af_heart`; the destination URL, a presigned R2 PUT URL for the item's audio key | Modal's call id for this synthesis, at once | 140 | fetch result | the call id | not ready while the synthesis runs; once it is done, the result below | 141 142 | Result field | Answers | 143 |---|---| 144 | format | which codec the audio is: `audio/ogg`, or `audio/wav` on the ffmpeg fallback | 145 | duration | the total audio length in seconds, what a progress bar divides by | 146 | timings | one `{start, end}` window per unit, in seconds, the last `end` equal to the duration; see [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md) | 147 148 The result carries no audio bytes, because the audio is already in the bucket under the item's audio key. The pipeline Worker declares the result's shape as a TypeScript type and trusts Modal's reply to match it; nothing checks it at runtime (see [common-package](common-package.md) for the rule the shared types follow). 149 150 > [!NOTE] Why Modal uploads the audio instead of returning it 151 > A Workflow step can return about 1 MiB, and a full article's audio is far larger. Handing Modal a presigned PUT URL keeps the audio out of the result, so the result endpoint answers with timing and metadata alone. The pipeline Worker signs the URL with an R2 API token of its own, using common/'s presigning function and its audio key function (see [common-package](common-package.md)). 152 153 > [!NOTE] Why proxy auth 154 > Modal's proxy auth rejects a request at Modal's edge, before any container starts. A shared key the app checks itself works too, but the web container has to start before it can reject the request. The pipeline Worker holds the proxy auth token as a secret. 155 156 ## 📩 Flow 157 158 ```mermaid 159 flowchart LR 160 P["paragraphs[]"] --> S["synthesize each
paragraph with Kokoro"] 161 S --> A["concatenate audio
+ 0.1s gaps"] 162 S --> T["build_timeline:
pause-fold windows"] 163 A --> E["encode: Opus,
WAV fallback"] 164 E --> U["upload to the
destination URL"] 165 U --> R["result: timeline
+ duration + format"] 166 T --> R 167 ``` 168 169 Each paragraph is synthesized independently through Kokoro-82M and its duration recorded, then the audios are concatenated with a fixed 0.1-second silence gap between them: none after the last paragraph, since there is nothing left to separate it from. [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md)'s `build_timeline` turns those per-paragraph durations into contiguous windows over the same concatenated audio. The encoded audio is uploaded to the destination URL, and the result Modal keeps for the call carries the timeline and the duration; the item Workflow joins the timeline onto the display markdown, described in [article-extraction](article-extraction.md), and never reads text back from the result. 170 171 > [!NOTE] A newline inside one paragraph string is Kokoro's own split, not this service's 172 > Kokoro splits a paragraph string at each newline before synthesizing it and joins those pieces back with no gap between them; the 0.1-second silence only sits between two separate entries of the `paragraphs` list. So a unit whose spoken form carries several lines, such as a list's items or a table's rows (see [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)), plays as one continuous paragraph audio with no silence added between its lines. The contract does not change. `paragraphs` stays `list[str]`, one string per unit, whether that string carries one line or several. 173 174 Audio is encoded to Opus through a `soundfile`-then-`ffmpeg` pipeline; if that codec path fails, it falls back to plain WAV. "Playable audio" is the only property either path is judged on, and WAV runs roughly 18 times larger than the equivalent Opus for a full article. 175 176 GPU and memory snapshotting are both enabled on the deployed class, bringing cold start down from roughly 27 seconds to roughly 6; a container then stays warm for 300 seconds after its last call, to absorb a session's burst of pushes. 177 178 ## 📡 How the item Workflow invokes it with no broker 179 180 ```mermaid 181 sequenceDiagram 182 autonumber 183 participant W as Item Workflow 184 participant M as Modal TTS 185 participant R as R2 bucket 186 W->>M: start synthesis with spoken forms, voice and PUT URL 187 M-->>W: call id 188 M->>R: PUT the encoded audio 189 loop until the result is ready 190 W->>M: fetch result for the call id 191 M-->>W: not ready, or timings, duration and format 192 end 193 ``` 194 195 The item Workflow's start synthesis step signs the PUT URL and calls the start endpoint, which spawns the synthesis and answers with Modal's call id at once (1, 2). Modal uploads the audio to the bucket when the synthesis finishes (3). The poll step asks the result endpoint for the call id until the result is ready (4, 5), and the store step writes the finished state into the item row together with the tts ledger row, priced by the audio's length (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) and [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md)). The call id and the result pass from step to step as step results; the item row holds neither. Each step gets 3 attempts: start synthesis has 2 minutes per attempt and each poll 1 minute. 196 197 A synthesis that fails every time fails the item once the poll step has used its attempts, and so does a result Modal has discarded, which happens 7 days after the call. 198 199 > [!WARNING] A start repeated after a deploy synthesizes twice 200 > Modal accepts no idempotency key and no caller-chosen call id, so a start synthesis step that runs again after a deploy spawns a second synthesis. Both upload to the same audio key, keyed by the item id, so the second upload overwrites the first and the item still has one audio file. The cost is one extra synthesis, which is accepted. 201 202 > [!NOTE] Why the compute platform is the async layer, and there is no broker 203 > The platform's own invocation primitives (spawn plus a non-blocking result read, exposed as the two endpoints) are sufficient async infrastructure at this scale: the running-versus-crashed distinction comes for free from the result read, not from anything the item Workflow tracks separately. The two deployables also ship independently: the TTS service ships on its own deploy cadence (see [deployment-and-ci](deployment-and-ci.md)), decoupled from the Workers. 204 205 > [!TIP] Rejected: a broker and a worker process 206 > A conventional task-queue stack, a message broker plus a separate worker, would add infrastructure to run, scale, and monitor for no benefit the platform's own spawn/poll primitives do not already provide, and it would still need the same crash/running bookkeeping the result read gives for free. 207 208 > [!NOTE] Clients poll; nothing pushes completion 209 > A client observes `generating` until the item Workflow writes `ready` or `failed` into the item row, and its next poll reads it. There is no notification path; see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) for the state machine this participates in. 210 211 The execution layer is coupled to Modal as a result: moving off it means replacing both the compute host and the async layer, and the GPU with them. 212 213 In local development Modal still runs in the cloud and uploads into the local bucket through a Cloudflare quick tunnel; [local-development](local-development.md) explains how the PUT URL reaches it. 214 215 ## ⏩ What is not built yet 216 217 Streaming paragraph audio from one warm container, so time-to-first-audio is roughly one to two seconds instead of waiting for the whole article. Word-level timestamps exist inside Kokoro but are not returned or used; a caption export would be the consumer that asks for them. 218 219 --- 220 221 Related: [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) · [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md) · [item-contract](item-contract.md) · [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md) · [common-package](common-package.md) · [local-development](local-development.md) · [deployment-and-ci](deployment-and-ci.md) · [invariants](invariants.md) 222 --- 223 title: "Authentication" 224 summary: "A single API key acts as the user's identity and guards every item route; audio and images reach a browser through a one-hour presigned R2 link the API Worker signs only for an authenticated caller." 225 created: "2026-07-29" 226 --- 227 228 # Authentication 229 230 ## 🔭 Overview 231 232 Items are private: an article someone enqueues is theirs, not public. A single API key is the user's identity, and it guards every route that touches an item. 233 234 ## ⚙️ Implementation details 235 236 The API Worker checks the key once, in front of every route under `/items`, so no handler checks it individually; a missing or wrong key answers `401`. The key is a secret only the API Worker holds. 237 238 Possessing the key **is** being the user: there is no separate identity, session, or login. The key is presented on an `X-API-Key` header and checked against the single configured value on every item route: creation, polling, retry, audio and images alike. `/health` is the one public route, and it carries no item data, a deliberate, narrow exception for platform health checks (see [deployment-and-ci](deployment-and-ci.md)). 239 240 > [!NOTE] Why one key rather than sessions or OAuth, for now 241 > The first consumer is an agent (Tachikoma), not a browser: it wants to present one credential on each call, not run an interactive login. There is no audience yet to onboard with real accounts; multi-user identity comes later, once anyone besides the owner wants this, and the private queue works for its first user without it. 242 243 ## 📩 How audio reaches a browser without the key 244 245 The audio and image routes require the key to **obtain** a link, and the audio route mints one only for a `ready` item. Each answers with a `307` to a GET URL for the object in the R2 bucket, signed by the API Worker with its own R2 API token for one hour, in every environment (see [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md)). The URL itself carries the signature, so the request that follows it needs no header at all. The bucket stays private: every way to read it is a link minted to an authenticated caller, and those links expire. 246 247 Only a backend holds the API key. A web app's own backend calls the route, takes the presigned URL from the `307`, and hands that URL to the browser. The audio route accepts no key in the query string, so the key never reaches a page. 248 249 ```mermaid 250 sequenceDiagram 251 participant Backend as Client backend 252 participant API as API Worker 253 participant R2 as R2 bucket 254 participant Browser 255 Backend->>API: GET /items/id/audio with X-API-Key 256 API->>API: key valid and item ready? 257 API->>API: sign a GET URL for one hour 258 API-->>Backend: 307 to the presigned URL 259 Backend-->>Browser: the presigned URL 260 Browser->>R2: GET the presigned URL, no header 261 R2-->>Browser: audio bytes 262 ``` 263 264 > [!NOTE] Why the route mints a link instead of gating the bytes 265 > A browser `

# Workflow testing: which test double replaces Firecrawl, Gemini and Modal

## Question

For a Workflow shaped like the item Workflow (fetch page, describe image, spawn TTS, sleep and poll TTS, write result, with D1 and R2 bindings), running under vitest and `@cloudflare/vitest-plugin` in workerd, which test double fits replacing Firecrawl, Gemini and Modal: step mocking through introspection, MSW intercepting `fetch` inside a step, or a code seam like today's `WORLD_SEAM`?

## Answer

All three work, with caveats, and they cover different things. Interception at the HTTP layer is the only kind that replays the existing cassettes, and it comes in two forms: MSW, and a fourth option found during the spike, miniflare's `outboundService`.

| | Step body runs | D1/R2 writes in the step | Client serialization and parsing | Replays `api/tests/cassettes` | Skips sleeps and retry delays |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Introspection `mockStepResult` / `mockStepError` / `forceStepTimeout` | no | no | no | no | yes, `disableSleeps` and `disableRetryDelays` |
| MSW in the test file | yes | yes | yes | yes, with a replayer, header stripping and URL rewriting | no, it needs introspection beside it |
| `outboundService` in the vitest config (Node side) | yes | yes | yes | yes, read straight from disk in Node | no, it needs introspection beside it |
| Code seam (`WORLD_SEAM`-style `ItemWorld`) | yes | yes | no, the double replaces the client | no | no, it needs introspection beside it |

Every combination ran green on plugin 1.1.13 (the repo's version) and on 1.3.6, three runs each with no flakes. Their behaviour did not differ.

Whatever double fills the step bodies, the plugin's introspection API is what removes the waits: `disableSleeps` and `disableRetryDelays` are the only way found to skip a `step.sleep` or a retry backoff. Without them a 30 s sleep takes 30 s of wall clock.

## What was run

The code is in `app/` (plugin 1.1.13, vitest 4.1.0, wrangler 4.135.0, workers-types 5.20260919.1, as in `pipeline/package.json`). `app-1.3.6/` is a copy with plugin 1.3.6, which brings in wrangler 4.147.0 and miniflare 5.20261001.

- `src/item-workflow.ts` holds `ItemWorkflow`. It runs `fetch page` (retries 2, 5 s constant), `describe image` (retries 3, 10 s exponential) and `spawn tts`, then loops `step.sleep("wait for tts", "30 seconds")` plus `poll tts`, which puts the audio in R2 when it is ready, and ends with `write result`. Every step updates the `items` row in D1.
- `src/clients.ts` holds plain `fetch` clients: Firecrawl `POST /v2/scrape`, Gemini `generateContent` with the image prompt from `api/`, and Modal `POST /submit` and `GET /result/{call_id}`, where 202 means still running.
- `src/world.ts` holds the `ItemWorld` seam, copied from the shape of `pipeline/src/workflow/world.ts`.
- `test/cassette.ts` holds a vcrpy YAML loader and an in-order replayer that matches on method and URI, with optional JSON body matching and URI rewriting.
- `test/fixtures.ts` imports three repo cassettes with Vite `?raw`: `test_firecrawl_fetch/test_firecrawl_http_surface`, `test_describe_images/test_image_describe_returns_a_clean_sentence` and `test_describe/test_a_429_retries_then_succeeds`. It also imports one fabricated Modal cassette, `test/cassettes/modal_tts_fabricated.yaml` (submit, 202, 202, 200 with an `X-Duration` header), because the repo has no Modal cassette: modal is mocked in the Python suite today.
- Tests: `test/introspection.test.ts`, `test/msw.test.ts` (msw 3.0.2), `test/msw2.test.ts` (msw 2.15.0), `test/seam.test.ts`, and `test/outbound/outbound.test.ts` under its own config, `vitest.outbound.config.ts`.

```
cd .scratch/cloudflare-migration/spikes/workflow-testing/app        # or app-1.3.6
pnpm install
pnpm vitest run --reporter=verbose --silent=false                   # 19 tests
pnpm vitest run -c vitest.outbound.config.ts --reporter=verbose     # 1 test
pnpm tsc --noEmit
```

No test reaches a real service, and no cloud resource was created.

## Measurements

| Test | Elapsed |
|---|---|
| Everything mocked through introspection, sleeps disabled | 22 ms |
| Two mocked errors on `describe image` with `disableRetryDelays` | 13–20 ms |
| One mocked error on `fetch page` without `disableRetryDelays` (5 s constant delay) | 5016 ms |
| One 30 s sleep not disabled (introspection test and seam test alike) | 30013 / 30024 ms |
| MSW replaying Firecrawl, Gemini and Modal through the real step bodies | 44–76 ms |
| `outboundService` replaying the same set | 61–117 ms |
| Whole suite, 19 tests, files in parallel | 38.6 s on both plugin versions, almost all of it the two deliberate 30 s sleeps |

MSW replay produced the same D1 row as the Python cassettes would imply: `title` "Herman Melville - Moby-Dick", `image_spoken` holding Gemini's recorded sentence about the Python logo, `tts_call_id` "fc-01SPIKE", status `ready`, and the R2 object holding the fabricated WAV bytes. The introspection run ended with `status = ready` while `title`, `image_spoken` and `tts_call_id` stayed `NULL`: only `write result`, the one step left unmocked, wrote to D1.

When a step exhausts its retries, the engine attempts it 1 + 5 times under the default retry config (counted from MSW misses on the unmatched Modal submit).

## Surprises

- **A falsy mocked result is ignored.** In miniflare's workflow engine, `mockStepResult` is applied by `else if (replaceResult)`, so a mocked `null`, `false`, `0` or `""` falls through and the real step body runs. In the first run, the step body made a real request to `nagara-tts-spike.modal.run` and got a 404. The spike's `poll tts` first returned `null` for "not yet"; it now returns `{ ready: false }` so it can be mocked. The behaviour is the same on both plugin versions.
- **An unmocked step reaches the real internet.** Introspection, MSW without a catch-all handler, and the seam all let anything they do not cover fall through to the network. One test sent the placeholder key to the live Gemini endpoint and got 400. Only `outboundService` sits in front of every outbound request.
- **`mockStepError` must come before `mockStepResult` on the same step.** In the other order, the modifier throws "Trying to mock error on step ... after mocking its result".
- **`getError()` drops the message of a `NonRetryableError`.** It returns `WorkflowFatalError: ... a step threw an NonRetryableError and it was not handled`; a plain error keeps its message, for example `{"message":"firecrawl 503"}`.
- **msw 3's `setupServer` from `msw/node` does not start in workerd.** Its `ClientRequest` interceptor reads `llhttp.wasm` from disk, and workerd's virtual filesystem cannot open the file (ENOENT). This holds on both plugin versions. msw 2.15's `msw/node` works as-is. msw 3 works through `msw/experimental`: `defineNetwork` with an `InterceptorSource` holding only `FetchInterceptor` (from `@mswjs/interceptors`, which has to be a direct dependency).
- **MSW and Workflow code share one global per test file.** The Workflow's `run()` executes in the test file's isolate, the same reason `WORLD_SEAM` on `globalThis` works today, so a patched `fetch` reaches inside `step.do`. Test files run in separate isolates: two files patching `fetch` concurrently did not interfere.
- **The Python cassettes do not replay verbatim.** vcrpy stores the decoded body next to the wire's `Content-Encoding: gzip` and `Content-Length`. Replaying both made workerd's `fetch` fail with "Decompression failed", and the Firecrawl step then burned through its retries. The replayer strips `content-encoding`, `content-length` and `transfer-encoding`.
- **Body matching works for Gemini and fails for Firecrawl.** The Gemini request rebuilt in TS from the same prompt and image matches the recorded body as JSON. The Firecrawl body does not, because the Python SDK sends nine fields the TS client does not (`origin: python-sdk@4.34.0`, `proxy`, `maxAge`, `blockAds` and others). Matching on URI alone is unsafe: in the `outboundService` run, the second interaction of the 429 cassette (a code-block describe) answered the image describe request, and the item went `ready` with "A Python function that wraps a single request." as its image description.
- **Going through the AI Gateway changes the URL.** The cassettes are recorded against `generativelanguage.googleapis.com`, and the Worker calls `gateway.ai.cloudflare.com/v1/{account}/{gateway}/google-ai-studio`. The replayer has to rewrite the URI.
- **`env` is shared and mutable between the test and the Workflow.** Overwriting `env.GEMINI_BASE` in a test changed the URL the step called.
- **msw's request type does not fit workers-types' `Request`.** Passing the request on needs `as unknown as Request`.
- **1.1.13 and 1.3.6 behave identically for every case above.** Neither exports a `fetchMock` from `cloudflare:test`. The undici `MockScope` types are still in the `.d.ts` file, but nothing exports them.

## Design decisions this raises

- Should the item Workflow's tests replay cassettes through the real step bodies (MSW or `outboundService`), stub at the step (introspection), stub behind a seam, or mix them per test? Today the API suite replays HTTP cassettes and the pipeline suite uses a seam.
- If cassettes: are the Python cassettes reused through a translating replayer (header stripping, URI rewrite, relaxed matching for Firecrawl), or re-recorded from the TS clients so that body matching holds?
- If interception: MSW in the test file, where handlers are per test and the module graph is the worker's, or `outboundService` in the config, where it runs in Node, reads cassettes from disk, blocks every unmatched request, and is controlled through a fake control host?
- If MSW: msw 2.15 with stock `msw/node`, or msw 3 with the experimental `defineNetwork` API?
- Is a test that lets an unmatched request reach the real network acceptable, or must the suite block unmatched requests the way `outboundService` does?

# item-workflow

## Question

What shape does the flattened item Workflow take on Cloudflare: the sleep-and-poll loop against the step limit, retries per step, and how a running item Workflow waits for and releases its domain's lease from a DomainQueue DO (today DomainQueue starts one Workflow per job)?

## Answer

Works, with caveats.

- **(a) TTS sleep-and-poll** is cheap against the step limit. A 12,128-word essay (70 min of audio, 176 s of synthesis) took 31 poll steps at a 5 s interval and 39 `step.do` steps for the whole item. At 5 s per poll, 10,000 steps would cover about 13.8 hours of synthesis.
- **(b) Retries per step** work as configured. A failure in a late step retries only that step, and earlier steps are not re-run. `instance.restart({ from: { name: "tts: submit" } })` on an errored item re-ran only from that step forward, which gives the retry route a shape. Caveat: a deploy made **every** step in flight fail with `WorkflowInternalError` (8 of 8 in round 8) and run its body again, even when the body had already finished. Sometimes the platform recorded that failure only when the step's timeout fired, up to 15 minutes later, and the lease stayed held the whole time.
- **(c) The lease** works both ways tried: the DO signals the waiter with `sendEvent` into `step.waitForEvent`, or the waiter polls the DO with `step.sleep` + a poll step. Handoffs were in FIFO order across concurrent items on one domain, and an item on another domain ran in parallel. Release worked on success (explicit step), on failure (try/catch in `run()`, or a rollback handler on the acquire step), and on termination (`terminate({rollback: true})` runs the rollback). A plain `terminate()` runs no code in the instance; the DO's alarm sweep frees the lease. An instance that dies mid-step (a deploy) keeps its lease, because its id is not terminal, and resumes holding it.

## Shape built

One Worker `nagara-spike-item-wf` with the item Workflow, a per-domain DomainQueue DO (`idFromName(domain)`, as in today's pipeline), D1 for item status and a per-attempt log, and R2 for audio. Code: `src/index.ts`.

Workflow steps, with the retry config used:

| Step name | Retries (limit, delay, backoff) | Timeout | What it does here |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fetch` | 3, 5 s, exponential | 2 min | Firecrawl `v2/scrape` markdown → paragraphs, or the paragraphs passed in params |
| `lease: request` | 5, 2 s, exponential | 30 s | `DomainQueue.acquire(itemId, mode)` → `{granted}` or `{granted:false, position}` |
| `lease: wait N` (waitForEvent, type `lease-granted`) / `lease: recheck N` | (recheck as above) | wait timeout 10 min | event variant: park until the DO signals; on timeout re-ask the DO |
| `lease: sleep N` / `lease: poll N` | 5, 2 s, exponential | 30 s | poll variant: sleep, then `acquire` again |
| `recipe` | 1, 5 s, constant | 15 min (configurable) | pass-through holding the lease for `holdSeconds` (stands in for the Flue agents) |
| `lease: release` | as lease | | `DomainQueue.release(itemId)` |
| `images`, `describe` | 2, 3 s, constant | 5 min | pass-through |
| `tts: submit` | 3, 10 s, exponential | 1 min | `POST /submit` on `nagara-tts-spike` (shared-key variant) |
| `tts: sleep N` / `tts: poll N` | 5, 5 s, linear | 30 s | `GET /result/{call_id}?part=meta`; 202 → keep looping |
| `store` | 3, 5 s, exponential | 2 min | `GET ?part=audio` streamed into `R2.put`; writes `ready`, duration and timing to D1 |
| `lease: release (failed)` | as lease | | `catch` in `run()` when release mode is `catch` |
| `mark failed` | default | | writes `failed` + error to D1, then rethrows |

Step names in loops carry a counter (`tts: poll 7`) because a repeated name replays the cached result. `wrangler workflows instances describe` shows them as `tts: poll 7-1`.

DomainQueue state: `lease {holder, mode, since}` and `waiting [{holder, mode}]` in the SQLite-backed sync KV (`ctx.storage.kv`), plus a log. The methods:

- `acquire(holder, mode)` is synchronous: it grants when the holder already holds the lease, or when the lease is free and the holder is first in line (or the line is empty). Otherwise it appends the holder and returns its position. With no `await` in the method, nothing can interleave.
- `release(holder, reason)` drops the holder from `waiting`, and if it holds the lease, deletes it and calls `advance()`. Release is keyed on the holder id, so a second release, or a release that arrives after the lease has moved on, is a no-op.
- `advance()` shifts the next waiter, checks `status()`, writes the lease to it and, for event waiters, calls `sendEvent({type: "lease-granted"})`. If `status()` is terminal or `sendEvent` throws, it skips to the next waiter. Poll waiters find the lease on their next poll.
- `alarm()` runs every `LEASE_ALARM_MS` (15 s here, 60 s in today's pipeline) while a lease is held. When the holder's status is `complete`/`errored`/`terminated`, or unaddressable, it sweeps the lease and calls `advance()`.

Release modes, chosen per item by a param:

- `catch`: `run()` wraps everything in try/catch; the catch runs `lease: release (failed)` and `mark failed`, then rethrows.
- `rollback`: `lease: request` registers a rollback handler that calls `release`. The handler runs when the instance fails, and on `terminate({ rollback: true })`.

## What was run

Routes on `https://nagara-spike-item-wf.asermax.workers.dev`: `POST /items` (params as JSON, `id` optional), `GET /items/{id}` (D1 row, instance status, attempt log), `POST /items/{id}/terminate[?rollback=1]`, `POST /items/{id}/restart?from=<step>`, `POST /items/{id}/clear-fault`, `GET /queue/{domain}`. Helpers: `post.sh` (enqueue a one-paragraph item), `show.sh` (print an item's timeline), `wait.sh` (block until instances are terminal). Raw output of every round is in `results/`.

| Round | What | Items |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Real item, Firecrawl → TTS | `r1-long` (paulgraham.com/greatwork.html) |
| 2 | 3 event waiters on `a.test`, 1 on `b.test`, 3 poll waiters on `c.test`, all at once, 20 s hold | `r2-*` |
| 3 | Long synthesis: the same essay, paragraphs extracted locally (231 paragraphs, 12,128 words); a deploy landed mid-poll | `r3-long` |
| 4 | Transient `describe` failure; `tts: submit` failing until cleared; `recipe` always failing with catch vs rollback, each with a waiter behind; holder terminated plainly + a waiter terminated; holder terminated with rollback; event sent 30 s before the waiter reaches `waitForEvent` | `r4-*` |

## Measurements

**(a) TTS loop and step count**

| Item | Audio | Synthesis (submit → store) | Poll steps | `step.do` steps total | Sleeps |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| r3-long, 231 paragraphs, 12,128 words | 4,217 s (70 min), 12.2 MB Opus in R2 | 176 s | 31 | 39 | 31 |
| one or two short paragraphs | 6-14 s | 6-15 s | 1-2 | 9-10 | 1-2 |

- Each poll took 0.2-0.4 s; 202 responses were fast. The poll that returned the 200 with metadata for the 70-min item took 1.9 s.
- The `store` step streamed the 12.2 MB file into R2 in 3.0 s. `ffprobe` on the R2 object reads 4,217.2 s. I did not listen to it.
- Polling at 5 s, the 10,000-step default allows about 13.8 h of synthesis per item; with exponential backoff it would allow far more.

**(b) Retries and resume**

- `describe` failing on attempts 1-2 (r5-transient, r6-t): attempts 2 and 3 ran 3.0 s apart, matching the `3 seconds` constant delay. `fetch`, `lease: request`, `recipe` and `images` each ran once.
- `tts: submit` failing on every attempt (r4-late): attempts landed at +10.9, +21.0, +41.2 and +81.4 s, matching 10 s exponential backoff (10, 20, 40 s). The step then threw, `run()` released the lease (already released after `recipe`, so a no-op) and wrote `failed`, and the instance ended `errored`.
- After clearing the fault, `restart({from: {name: "tts: submit"}})` resumed r4-late: `tts: submit` ran again as attempt 1, then poll and store, and the item reached `ready`. `fetch`, `lease`, `recipe`, `images` and `describe` did not run again. The D1 `error` column still held the old error, because the spike never clears it.

**(c) Lease handoff**

| Case | What happened |
|---|---|
| 3 event waiters on one domain (r2, r5) | FIFO order. Release → `sendEvent` 0.3-0.5 s → the next item's `recipe` starts within about a second |
| 3 poll waiters on one domain (r2, r7) | FIFO order. Release → pickup on the next poll, 0-5 s. A waiter spends one step per 5 s of waiting: 9 poll steps for a 47 s wait (r7-po-3) |
| Another domain at the same time | Ran in parallel, never queued |
| Holder fails in `recipe`, catch mode (r4/r5) | `lease: release (failed)` ran 0.2 s after the last attempt and the waiter was granted 0.5 s later |
| Holder fails in `recipe`, rollback mode (r4-rb-1) | The rollback handler on `lease: request` ran 0.2 s after the last attempt and the waiter was granted 0.5 s later |
| Holder `terminate()` without rollback (r4-term-1) | No code ran in the instance. The alarm swept the lease when it next fired; here that was 1.4 s after the terminate, because the alarm happened to be due. The worst case is `LEASE_ALARM_MS` |
| A waiter terminated while queued (r4-term-2) | `status()` still reported it as not terminal about 1 s after the terminate; `sendEvent` threw `(instance.in_finite_state) Instance reached a finite state, cannot send events to it`; the DO skipped it and granted the next waiter |
| Holder `terminate({rollback: true})` (r4-termrb-1) | The rollback handler released the lease 13 s after the terminate call |
| Event sent before the waiter reached `waitForEvent` (r4-early-2, r5-early-2) | The event was kept: `waitForEvent` returned at once when the waiter got there (20-30 s later) |

## Surprises

- **A deploy fails every step that is executing** (rounds 4, 6, 7, 8). Each such attempt is recorded as `WorkflowInternalError: Attempt failed due to internal workflows error`, and the step body runs again. That attempt counts against the step's retry limit: `recipe` has `limit: 1`, so a real failure on the re-run would have exhausted it. The body is re-executed even when it had already finished. In r4-late, `recipe` logged `ok` at +4.0 s and ran again at +6.5 s. Step bodies must therefore be idempotent: the recipe step's D1 write, `tts: submit` (a second Modal call), and R2 puts.
- **When the platform records that failure varies.** Of the 8 steps in round 8, 5 were marked failed as soon as their body finished (about 42 s). One was marked failed at its 2-minute timeout, one at its 15-minute timeout, and one at 5:00, which matches neither. In round 7, r7-ev-2 held the lease for 15 minutes this way while a waiter queued behind it, and the waiter's 10-minute `lease: recheck 1` found the lease still held. The step timeout bounds the stall in the cases seen, except the 5:00 one.
- **`waitForEvent` across a deploy**: twice (r4-catch-2, r6-2) the event reached the instance at send time (the step's output carries the send timestamp), but the step ended exactly 5:00 after the wait began. Without a deploy nearby (rounds 2, 4's other cases, 5), waits resolved in under a second.
- **Poll waiters sleeping across a deploy were not delayed** (r7-po-2/3, 6 and 9 polls, all 5 s apart). The deploy did not disturb `r3-long` either, which was mid TTS loop.
- **`status()` does not tell a parked waiter from a running one**: the DO saw `running` for instances inside `waitForEvent` in most handoffs, and `waiting` in some (r6-3, r7-ev-3).
- **A deterministic TTS failure is retried as if transient.** In r1-long, one Firecrawl paragraph made Kokoro raise `ValueError: need at least one array to concatenate` (`_synth_paragraph`, line 61 of the spike app). `/result` then answered 500 on every poll, and the `tts: poll 14` step retried 5 times over 76 s before the item failed. The modal-http endpoint returns no status that marks a failed call as distinct from a broken poll.
- Rollback handlers and `restart({from})` exist in the runtime and types (rollbacks added June 2026). Neither appears in the global wiki entry on Workflows.

"""Nagara TTS service — Kokoro-82M on Modal.

Accepts paragraphs[] and returns per-paragraph {index, start, end, text} timing plus
the encoded audio. Runs as its own Modal app, separate from the API, which invokes it
remotely.

Deploy:  uv run modal deploy app.py
"""

import modal

app = modal.App("nagara-tts")

SR = 24000
PAUSE_S = 0.1  # inter-paragraph silence — enough to mark the break without stalling the prose


def build_timeline(durations: list[float], pause_s: float) -> list[dict]:
    """Cumulative per-paragraph windows. The inter-paragraph pause is folded into the
    *preceding* paragraph's end, so windows are contiguous and the last `end` equals the
    total audio duration (sum of durations + (n-1) pauses)."""
    timeline, t, n = [], 0.0, len(durations)
    for i, dur in enumerate(durations):
        end = t + dur + (pause_s if i < n - 1 else 0.0)
        timeline.append({"index": i, "start": t, "end": end})
        t = end
    return timeline


def _bake():
    from kokoro import KPipeline

    list(KPipeline(lang_code="a")("warm up", voice="af_heart"))


image = (
    modal.Image.debian_slim(python_version="3.12")
    .apt_install("espeak-ng", "ffmpeg")
    .pip_install("kokoro==0.9.4", "soundfile", "torch", "numpy")
    .run_function(_bake)
)


@app.cls(
    image=image,
    gpu="L4",
    scaledown_window=300,  # stay warm across a session's burst of pushes
    enable_memory_snapshot=True,
    experimental_options={"enable_gpu_snapshot": True},  # ~27s -> ~6s cold start
)
class Kokoro:
    @modal.enter(snap=True)
    def load(self):
        from kokoro import KPipeline

        self.pipeline = KPipeline(lang_code="a")

    def _synth_paragraph(self, text, voice):
        import numpy as np

        audio = np.concatenate([a for _, _, a in self.pipeline(text, voice=voice)])
        return audio, len(audio) / SR

    def _encode_opus(self, audio):
        import io
        import subprocess

        import soundfile as sf

        wav = io.BytesIO()
        sf.write(wav, audio, SR, format="WAV")
        try:
            opus = subprocess.run(
                ["ffmpeg", "-y", "-loglevel", "error", "-i", "pipe:0",
                 "-c:a", "libopus", "-b:a", "24k", "-ac", "1", "-f", "ogg", "pipe:1"],
                input=wav.getvalue(), stdout=subprocess.PIPE, check=True,
            ).stdout
            return opus, "audio/ogg"
        except Exception:
            # WAV fallback if the codec path snags — "playable" is the judged property
            return wav.getvalue(), "audio/wav"

    @modal.method()
    def synthesize(self, paragraphs: list[str], voice: str = "af_heart"):
        import numpy as np

        gap = np.zeros(int(SR * PAUSE_S), dtype=np.float32)

        audios, durations = [], []
        for para in paragraphs:
            audio, dur = self._synth_paragraph(para, voice)
            audios.append(audio)
            durations.append(dur)

        chunks = []
        for i, audio in enumerate(audios):
            chunks.append(audio)
            if i < len(audios) - 1:
                chunks.append(gap)
        full = np.concatenate(chunks)

        timeline = build_timeline(durations, PAUSE_S)
        for entry, para in zip(timeline, paragraphs):
            entry["text"] = para

        audio_bytes, fmt = self._encode_opus(full)

        import base64

        return {
            "audio_base64": base64.b64encode(audio_bytes).decode(),
            "format": fmt,
            "sample_rate": SR,
            "duration": len(full) / SR,
            "paragraphs": timeline,
        }

# CI for the pipeline/ subproject: test, lint, and types run in parallel on
# pushes to main; a deploy job runs only after all three pass, building the
# Worker through the Vite/Flue pipeline and deploying with wrangler-action.
# Path-filtered to pipeline/** so unrelated changes don't trigger it (the same
# isolation the api and tts workflows enforce).
#
# This file is written per the settled design (mirroring tts.yml, whose deploy
# job is likewise gated on all three checks); it deploys nothing from this
# environment and needs the CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN secret to ever run.
#
# Deploy auth: set CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN (and CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID if the
# token is scoped across accounts) as GitHub Actions secrets.
name: pipeline

on:

import { init } from "@flue/runtime";
import type * as v from "valibot";
import { Author, type AuthorInitialData } from "./author.ts";
import { Revisor, type RevisorInitialData } from "./revisor.ts";

export type AgentKind = "author" | "revision";

export interface AgentDispatchReceipt {
  submissionId: string;
  acceptedAt: string;
  uid: string;
}

export interface AgentInitialData {
  html: string;
  recipe?: string;
}

function agentFor(kind: AgentKind) {
  return kind === "author" ? Author : Revisor;
}

function initialDataFor(kind: AgentKind, data: AgentInitialData): unknown {
  if (kind === "author") {
    return { html: data.html } satisfies v.InferOutput<typeof AuthorInitialData>;
  }
  return { html: data.html, recipe: data.recipe ?? "" } satisfies v.InferOutput<
    typeof RevisorInitialData
  >;
}

export async function dispatchAgent(
  kind: AgentKind,
  conversationId: string,
  message: string,
  initialData: AgentInitialData,
): Promise<AgentDispatchReceipt> {
  const handle = init(agentFor(kind), { id: conversationId });
  return await handle.dispatch({ message, initialData: initialDataFor(kind, initialData) });
}

export async function readAgent(
  kind: AgentKind,
  conversationId: string,
  receipt: AgentDispatchReceipt,
): Promise<{ text: string }> {
  const handle = init(agentFor(kind), { id: conversationId });
  const reply = await handle.read(receipt);
  return { text: reply.text };
}
# Cassettes over mocks

The api suite replays a service behind an HTTP boundary, the extraction pipeline, from cassettes exactly as it replays firecrawl and gemini, so the client's real serialization and parsing run against the recorded shapes. Mocks are for calls that are not plain HTTP.

- Record against the real service when it can run: `wrangler dev` needs no account and serves on localhost. The conftest's matching rules carry the hard parts: body matching disambiguates POSTs to one URL, and repeated identical GETs replay in recorded order, which is a poll sequence.
- Fabricate when the service does not exist yet: a cassette is YAML of request and response pairs, hand-built from the boundary contract. The trade is that a recorded cassette is evidence the service answered, and a fabricated one is the contract restated as a fixture, so drift passes unnoticed. Both sides are ours, so the risk is small.
- The unreachable case cannot be a cassette: a refused connection produces no interaction. Point the client at 127.0.0.1, a closed port that refuses instantly, with recording disabled for that one test. The failure is a genuine network one.
- Mocks stay for what is not HTTP: modal's spawn-and-resolve, the gemini describer SDK.
- Volatile ids break replay: minted `itm_` handles differ per run. A registered matcher normalizes them on both sides, cassette and request, so one cassette replays across any mint.

### 3.3 Critical behaviour

The re-queue claims the row with one conditional UPDATE before it touches the instance, the same pattern as the retry claim, so two polls landing together restart the instance once. It does not increment `retry_count`: the cap bounds client retries of failed items, and a re-queue recovers an item that never failed. It restarts from `restartPoint(current_step)`, so an item waiting for its domain's lease (current_step `lease`) asks for the lease again, and DomainQueue keeps an id that is already in its FIFO at its position (5.1); a re-queue never sends a waiting item to the back.

The retry route reaches the same `restartPoint`. `recipe` and `release` map to `lease`; `poll <n>` restarts at that poll step, so the poll steps before it replay from cache and Modal is not asked to synthesize again; an empty `current_step` restarts every step.

Neither route reads the instance's status: the row is the only state the API reads, as the design says.

### 4.1 Control flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    start(["ItemWorkflow.run<br/>params {itemId}"]) --> s1["1 fetch · queued<br/>writes instance id,<br/>domain, ledger row<br/>returns {html}"]
    s1 --> s2["2 lease · queued<br/>ask DomainQueue,<br/>waitForEvent lease-granted"]
    s2 --> s3["3 recipe · generating<br/>run, author or revise;<br/>spoken form and drop;<br/>writes title, units"]
